empires.historical_map_title: The First Empire — India under the Mauryas (c. 322–185 BCE)

detailed_history.overview: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya with the strategic counsel of Chanakya (Kautilya) in 322 BCE, the Mauryan Empire became the largest state ever established in the Indian subcontinent, spanning 5,000,000 km² from the Hindu Kush (Kandahar and Herat) to the borders of the Tamil realms. Under Ashoka the Great (r. 268–232 BCE), the empire embraced universal non-violence (Ahimsa), civic welfare, and the propagation of Dhamma across Asia and the Mediterranean.

chronicle.era: c. 322 – 297 BCE: Chandragupta Maurya & Seleucid Treaty
chronicle.narrative: Overthrowing the Nanda dynasty at Pataliputra, Chandragupta repelled the invasion of Seleucus I Nicator in 305 BCE. The resulting treaty ceded Arachosia (Kandahar), Gedrosia (Balochistan), and Paropamisadae (Kabul) to the Mauryas in exchange for 500 war elephants, sealed by a diplomatic marriage and the appointment of Megasthenes as Greek ambassador.

chronicle.era: c. 297 – 268 BCE: Bindusara & Trans-Peninsular Expansion
chronicle.narrative: Known to the Greeks as Amitrochates (Slayer of Foes), Bindusara extended imperial suzerainty southward into the Deccan plateau, maintaining diplomatic correspondences with Antiochus I Soter of Syria and Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt.

chronicle.era: c. 268 – 232 BCE: Ashoka the Great & Imperial Dhamma
chronicle.narrative: In 261 BCE, Ashoka conquered Kalinga in a catastrophic war resulting in 100,000 casualties and 150,000 captives. Overcome by profound remorse, Ashoka renounced aggressive conquest (Digvijaya) in favor of moral conquest through righteousness (Dharmavijaya). He inscribed 33 Major and Minor Rock and Pillar Edicts across India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan in Prakrit (Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts), Greek, and Aramaic.

primary_sources.source_title: Ashoka Major Rock Edict XIII (Kālsī / Shāhbāzgaṛhī Version)
primary_sources.original_text: अठ-वसाभिसितस देवानंपियस पियदसिनो लाजिनो कलिग्या विजिता । दियढ-मित्रे पाण-सहसे ये ततो अपवुढे, सत-सहस-मित्रे तत हते, बहु-तावते वा मठे । ततो पछा अधुना लधेषु कलिगेषु तीवे धंम-वाये धंम-कामता धंमानुसथि चा देवानंपियस । सो अथि अनुसोचने देवानंपियस विजिति कलिग्यानि ॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Aṭha-vasābhisitasa Devānaṁpiyasa Piyadasino lājino Kaligyā vijitā | Diyaḍha-mitre pāṇa-sahase ye tato apavuḍhe, sata-sahasa-mitre tata hate, bahu-tāvate vā maṭhe | Tato pachā adhunā ladheṣu Kaligeṣu tīve dhaṁma-vāye dhaṁma-kāmatā dhaṁmānusathi cā Devānaṁpiyasa | So athi anusocane Devānaṁpiyasa vijiti Kaligyāni ||
primary_sources.translation: In the eighth year of his consecration, the Beloved of the Gods, King Priyadarsin, conquered Kalinga. One hundred and fifty thousand persons were carried away captive, one hundred thousand were slain, and many times that number perished. Thereafter, now that Kalinga is annexed, the Beloved of the Gods has turned eagerly toward the practice, love, and instruction of Dhamma. The Beloved of the Gods sorrows profoundly for the conquest of Kalinga.
primary_sources.academic_citation: E. Hultzsch, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. I: Inscriptions of Asoka, Archaeological Survey of India, 1925, pp. 66–70, 206–211; Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas, Oxford University Press, 1997.
primary_sources.significance: The single most moving personal royal confession and unilateral imperial renunciation of war preserved from antiquity.

primary_sources.source_title: Megasthenes, Indika (Fragm. 34, preserved in Strabo XV.1.50–52)
primary_sources.original_text: Τῶν δ' ἀρχόντων οἱ μὲν ἀγορανόμοι εἰσίν, οἱ δ' ἀστυνόμοι, οἱ δ' ἐπὶ τῶν στρατιωτῶν... οἱ δ' ἀστυνόμοι εἰς ἓξ πεντάδας διαιροῦνται· οἱ μὲν τὰ δημιουργικὰ σκοποῦσιν, οἱ δὲ ξενοδοχοῦσιν, οἱ δὲ γενέσεις καὶ τελευτὰς ἀπογράφουσιν...
primary_sources.transliteration: Tōn d' archontōn hoi men agoranomoi eisin, hoi d' astynomoi, hoi d' epi tōn stratiōtōn... hoi d' astynomoi eis hex pentadas diairountai: hoi men ta dēmiourgika skopousin, hoi de xenodochousin, hoi de geneseis kai teleutas apographousin...
primary_sources.translation: Of the governing officials at Pataliputra, some oversee agriculture and forestry, others the army, and thirty commissioners oversee the municipality divided into six boards of five members each: the first inspects handicrafts, the second receives foreigners, the third registers births and deaths to ensure equitable tax collection, the fourth controls retail trade and measures, the fifth inspects manufactured goods, and the sixth collects the tithe on sales.
primary_sources.academic_citation: J.W. McCrindle, Ancient India as Described by Megasthenes and Arrian, Chuckervertty, Chatterjee & Co., 1926, pp. 86–91; Strabo, Geographica, Book XV (Loeb Classical Library, 1930).
primary_sources.significance: Eye-witness western documentary proof of the sophisticated urban bureaucracy and census accounting governing the Mauryan capital.

locations.name: Pataliputra
locations.role: Imperial seat of the Mauryas; city of 64 gates and 570 towers
locations.desc: Monumental wooden and stone-pillared palatial capital described by Megasthenes.

locations.name: Taxila (Uttarapatha)
locations.role: Northern viceroyalty headquarters; Pan-Asian academy
locations.desc: Governed by crown princes including Ashoka; nexus of Silk Road and Uttarapatha trade.

locations.name: Ujjayini (Avantiratha)
locations.role: Western viceroyalty headquarters on international highway
locations.desc: Governed by Ashoka as viceroy; center of astronomical study and western trade.

locations.name: Tosali (Dhauli / Kalinga)
locations.role: Eastern viceroyalty following the Kalinga War
locations.desc: Seat of the Kumara (royal prince) and site of Ashoka's Separate Rock Edicts at Dhauli.

locations.name: Suvarnagiri (Dakshinapatha)
locations.role: Southern viceroyalty in Karnataka
locations.desc: Headquarters of the southern province managing royal gold mines (Hatti gold belt).

locations.name: Alexandropolis / Kandahar
locations.role: Northwestern bilingual Ashokan rock edict site
locations.desc: Greek and Aramaic bilingual inscriptions by Ashoka commanding piety and vegetarianism.

locations.name: Girnar (Junagadh)
locations.role: Western provincial fortress and Sudarshana Lake dam
locations.desc: Engineered under Chandragupta by governor Pushyagupta and canalized under Ashoka by Tushaspha.

locations.name: Sannati
locations.role: Major Karnataka stupa complex with inscribed Ashokan portrait
locations.desc: Only known sculpted portrait inscribed 'Raya Asoko' discovered at Kanaganahalli.

locations.name: Sopara (Shurparaka)
locations.role: Chief Mauryan port on the Arabian Sea
locations.desc: Site of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts VIII and IX engraved on basalt blocks.

locations.name: Tamralipti
locations.role: Eastern oceanic emporium on the Bay of Bengal
locations.desc: Port from which Princess Sanghamitta embarked carrying a sapling of the Bodhi tree to Sri Lanka.

locations.name: Sarnath (Isipatana)
locations.role: Site of the Lion Capital of Ashoka (National Emblem of India)
locations.desc: Erected by Ashoka to commemorate Buddha's First Sermon (Dharmachakrapravartana).

locations.name: Lumbini (Rummindei)
locations.role: Birthplace of Gautama Buddha
locations.desc: Ashoka's pillar inscription recording royal tax exemption ('lummini-game ubalike kate').

locations.name: Brahmagiri
locations.role: Southern Karnataka Minor Rock Edict site
locations.desc: Engraved by royal scribe Chapada in both Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts.

locations.name: Maski
locations.role: Edict confirming Ashoka's personal name
locations.desc: Famous Minor Rock Edict directly naming 'Devanampriya Asoka' discovered in 1915.

locations.name: Shravanabelagola
locations.role: Chandragupta Maurya's ascetic retirement sanctuary
locations.desc: Chandragiri hill where Emperor Chandragupta undertook the Jain rite of Sallekhana with Bhadrabahu.

empires.name: Post-Mauryan & Indo-Greek Kingdoms

capitals.name: Vidisha (Besnagar)
capitals.role: Primary Shunga imperial capital and cultural center
capitals.desc: Seat of Crown Prince Agnimitra; site of the Heliodorus Garuda pillar.

capitals.name: Pataliputra
capitals.role: Eastern Shunga imperial seat
capitals.desc: Retained as imperial capital by Pushyamitra Shunga following the Mauryan overthrow.

capitals.name: Sagala (Sialkot)
capitals.role: Indo-Greek capital of King Menander I (Milinda)
capitals.desc: Cosmopolitan Greco-Indian city celebrated for parks, moats, and Buddhist stupas in Milinda Panha.

capitals.name: Pushkalavati (Charsadda)
capitals.role: Western Indo-Greek mint and fortified administrative center
capitals.desc: Center of Hellenistic minting and Gandharan stone craft.

boundary_phases.phase: Menander I's Peak Indo-Greek Realm (c. 150 BCE)
boundary_phases.description: Menander I (Milinda) ruled from the Paropamisadae and Arachosia across the Punjab to the Yamuna, striking refined bilingual silver drachms bearing Greek and Kharosthi inscriptions.

boundary_phases.phase: Shunga Empire in Central & Eastern India (c. 175 BCE)
boundary_phases.description: Pushyamitra Shunga revived Vedic Ashvamedha sacrifices and patronized the reconstruction of the Sanchi Stupa gateways and Bharhut balustrades.

neighboring_kingdoms.name: Satavahanas of Deccan
neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Satavahanas of Deccan: Contemporaneous frontier realm and trading partner.

neighboring_kingdoms.name: Kharavela of Kalinga
neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Maritime eastern kingdom noted for elephant cavalry and oceanic trade with Southeast Asia.

neighboring_kingdoms.name: Indo-Scythians (Sakas)
neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Indo-Scythian rulers of Gujarat, Malwa, and Saurashtra; issued refined silver coinage.

battles.name: Battle of the Sindhu River
battles.parties: Prince Vasumitra (Shunga) vs. Indo-Greek Yavana Cavalry
battles.summary: Pushyamitra's grandson Vasumitra guarded the imperial sacrificial horse on the banks of the Sindhu, repelling Greek cavalry in a fierce engagement.

battles.name: Indo-Greek Siege of Saketa (Ayodhya)
battles.parties: Indo-Greek King (Demetrius / Menander) vs. Shunga Garrison
battles.summary: Yavana armies advanced deep into the Gangetic heartland, laying siege to Saketa and Mathura as recorded by the grammarian Patanjali.

battles.name: Greco-Bactrian March on Pataliputra
battles.parties: Menander I of Sagala vs. Shunga Imperial Forces
battles.summary: Menander's allied vanguard reached the mud-brick fortifications of Pataliputra before civil conflicts in Bactria forced the Greeks to retreat.

battles.name: Menander's Conquest of Mathura
battles.parties: Menander I vs. Surasena Chieftains
battles.summary: Indo-Greek annexation of the upper Yamuna valley, leaving hoards of Menander's silver drachms across the Mathura region.
battles.source: Archaeological Survey of India Coin Hoards

battles.name: Shunga–Vidarbha War
battles.parties: Crown Prince Agnimitra vs. King Yajnasena of Vidarbha
battles.summary: Agnimitra's general Virasena crossed the Narmada and defeated Yajnasena, partitioning Vidarbha between two cousin-rulers subject to Shunga suzerainty.

battles.name: Defense of Pushyamitra's Ashvamedha
battles.parties: Imperial Shunga Army vs. Regional Insurgents
battles.summary: Pushyamitra successfully concludes his second Ashvamedha sacrifice, reaffirming Vedic imperial rituals across northern India.

events.title: Pushyamitra Shunga Founds the Shunga Empire at Pataliputra & Vidisha
events.desc: Restores Vedic court rituals while presiding over monumental stone stupas and commercial prosperity along central India.

shloka.text: कोसलाधिपेन द्विरश्वमेधयाजिनः सेनापतेः पुष्यमित्रस्य षष्ठेन धनदेवेन धर्मराज्ञा पितुः फल्गुदेवस्य केतनं कारितम् ॥
shloka.transliteration: Kosalādhipena dvir-aśvamedhayājinaḥ senāpateḥ Puṣyamitrasya ṣaṣṭhena Dhanadevena dharmarājñā pituḥ Phalgudevasya ketanaṁ kāritam ||
shloka.translation: By Dhanadeva, righteous lord of Kosala, sixth in descent from General Pushyamitra who performed two Ashvamedha horse sacrifices, was this memorial monument erected.
shloka.citation: Ayodhyā Stone Inscription of King Dhanadeva

events.title: Demetrius I Crosses the Hindu Kush into Gandhara & Punjab
events.desc: Greco-Bactrian forces establish fortified twin-axis cities at Sirkap (Taxila) and Demetrias in Sind, minting bilingual Attic/Indian coinage.

shloka.text: यो सहस्सं सहस्सेन सङ्गामे मानुसे जिने । एकं च जेय्यमत्तानं स वे सङ्गामजुत्तमो ॥
shloka.transliteration: Yo sahassaṁ sahassena saṅgāme mānuse jine | Ekañca jeyyamattānaṁ sa ve saṅgāmajuttamo ||
shloka.translation: Though one conquer a million warriors upon the battlefield, he who masters his own spirit is the noblest victor of all.

events.title: Prince Vasumitra Guards Pushyamitra's Ashvamedha Horse on the Sindhu
events.desc: Immortalized in Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram, young Vasumitra defeats Yavana cavalry patrols defending the imperial ritual steed.

shloka.text: इह अधीमहे, इह वसामः, इह पुष्यमित्रं याजयामः ॥
shloka.transliteration: iha adhīmahe, iha vasāmaḥ, iha Puṣyamitraṁ yājayāmaḥ ||
shloka.translation: Here we study, here we dwell, and here we officiate at the Ashvamedha sacrifice of Emperor Pushyamitra.

events.title: Agathocles Mints Bilingual Brahmi Coins Honoring Balarama & Vasudeva
events.desc: Issues square copper coins at Ai-Khanoum and Taxila depicting Balarama and Vasudeva Krishna in early Brahmi alongside Greek script.

shloka.text: रजेने अगथुक्लेयेस... वासुदेव-सङ्कर्षणौ देवौ लोकस्य रक्षकौ ॥
shloka.transliteration: Rajane Agathukleyesa (Brahmi Coin Legend) — Vāsudeva-Saṅkarṣaṇau lokasya rakṣakau ||
shloka.translation: Bilingual square drachms inscribed 'Of King Agathocles' in Early Brahmi portray Balarama with plough and Krishna Vasudeva with discus.
shloka.citation: Agathocles Ai-Khanoum Bilingual Drachm Corpus (c. 180–170 BCE)
shloka.lang: Prakrit / Greek · Early Brahmi & Attic Greek

events.title: Consecration of the Stone Toranas & Medallions at Bharhut Stupa
events.desc: Master artisans of the Shunga realm transform timber stupa gates into narrative sandstone reliefs depicting Jatakas and royal processions.

shloka.text: सुगनं रजे रञो गागीपुतस विसदेवस पौतेण... इदं तोरणं सिलकंमं त च उप्पनं ॥
shloka.transliteration: Suganaṁ raje raño Gāgīputasa Visadevasa pauteṇa... idaṁ toraṇaṁ silakaṁmaṁ ca uppanaṁ ||
shloka.translation: During the sovereignty of the Shungas, this carved sandstone gateway (Torana) and ornamental medallion stonework were raised by pious patrons at Bharhut.
shloka.citation: Bharhut Stūpa East Gateway Inscription of Dhanabhūti

events.title: King Menander I (Milinda) Unifies Punjab & Reaches Mathura
events.desc: From his bustling capital at Sagala (Sialkot), Menander mints brilliant silver drachms in Greek and Kharosthi styling himself 'Soter' and 'Dharmika'.

shloka.text: महाराजस त्रतारस ध्रमिकस मेनद्रस ॥ (ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΣΩΤΗΡΟΣ ΜΕΝΑΝΔΡΟΥ)
shloka.transliteration: Mahārājasa trātārasa dhramikasa Menandrasa (Kharoṣṭhī Reverse Legend of Menander I)
shloka.translation: 'Of the Great King Menander, the Savior and Follower of Dharma'—inscribed across silver drachms linking Punjab with Hellenistic Bactria.
shloka.citation: Menander I (Milinda) Bilingual Tetradrachms & Kharosthi Coinage

events.title: Sage Patanjali Composes the Vyākaraṇa Mahābhāṣya
events.desc: Citing 'Here we sacrifice for Pushyamitra' as a contemporaneous grammatical example, Patanjali completes India's monumental Sanskrit linguistic commentary.

shloka.text: अथ शब्दानुशासनम् । केषां शब्दानाम् । लौकिकानां वैदिकानां च ॥
shloka.transliteration: atha śabdānuśāsanam | keṣāṁ śabdānām? laukikānāṁ vaidikānāṁ ca ||
shloka.translation: Now commences the systematic science of words—encompassing both the living spoken speech of the people and the sacred Vedic hymns.

events.title: Philosophical Dialogues of Milindapañha at Sagala
events.desc: King Menander debates Buddhist monk Nagasena across subtle questions of self, ethics, and statecraft, embracing the Dhamma.

shloka.text: न हि वेरेन वेरानि सम्मन्तीध कुदाचनं । अवेरेन च सम्मन्ति एस धम्मो सनन्तनो ॥
shloka.transliteration: Na hi verena verāni sammantīdha kudācanaṁ | Averena ca sammanti esa dhammo sanantano ||
shloka.translation: Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world; by non-hatred alone is hatred pacified—this is the eternal law.

events.title: Vidisha Civic & Ivory-Carvers' Guilds Fund Sanchi Monumental Art
events.desc: Organized artisanal shrenis in Malwa sponsor narrative sculptures uniting urban commerce with sacred patronage.

shloka.text: वेदिसाकेहि दंतकारेहि रूपकम्मं कतं ॥
shloka.transliteration: Vedisākehi dantakārehi rūpakammaṁ kataṁ ||
shloka.translation: This intricate narrative stone relief work upon the southern gateway was sculpted and endowed by the ivory-carvers' guild of Vidisha.
shloka.citation: Sanchi Stūpa I South Gateway Guild Inscription

events.title: Expansion & Dressed Sandstone Railings of the Great Stupa at Sanchi
events.desc: Under Shunga patronage, civic guilds from Vidisha double the brick core of Sanchi Stupa I and encase it in dressed sandstone.

shloka.text: यथा हि रथसम्बन्धात् सङ्ख्या गच्छति संवृतिम् । एवं धर्मसमायोगात् पुण्यकीर्तिः प्रवर्धते ॥
shloka.transliteration: yathā hi rathasambandhāt saṅkhyā gacchati saṁvṛtim | evaṁ dharmasamāyogāt puṇyakīrtiḥ pravardhate ||
shloka.translation: Just as the word 'chariot' arises only when axle, wheel, and frame unite, so civil harmony flourishes through ethical interdependence.

events.title: Heliodorus, Greek Envoy from Taxila, Erects Garuda Pillar at Vidisha
events.desc: Ambassador Heliodorus proclaims himself a 'Bhagavata' in Early Brahmi and inscribes ethical tenets drawn from the Mahabharata.

shloka.text: देवदेवस वासुदेवस गरुडध्वजे अयं कारिते इअ हेलियोदोरेण भागवतेन... त्रीणि अमृतपदानि सु-अनुष्ठितानि नयन्ति स्वर्गम्—दम त्याग अप्रमाद ॥
shloka.transliteration: Devadevasa Vāsudevasa garuḍadhvaje ayaṁ kārite ia Heliodoreṇa bhāgavatena... trīṇi amṛtapadāni su-anuṣṭhitāni nayanti svargam—dama tyāga apramāda ||
shloka.translation: This Garuda pillar of Vasudeva was erected by Heliodorus, Greek envoy from Taxila and devotee of Vishnu... Three immortal steps lead to heaven: Self-restraint, Renunciation, and Vigilance.
shloka.citation: Heliodorus Pillar Inscription, Besnagar (Vidisha, c. 113 BCE)

events.title: Kanva Transition & Indo-Scythian Satrapies in Taxila & Mathura
events.desc: Minister Vasudeva Kanva succeeds the Shungas in Magadha, while Maues and Rajuvula establish Saka satrapies across Punjab and Mathura.

shloka.text: माथुरे सिंहशीर्षे... सकस्तनस पूजये सर्वबुद्धानं सर्वसत्वानं च हितसुखाय ॥
shloka.transliteration: Māthure Siṁhaśīrṣe... Sakastanasa pūjaye sarvabuddhānaṁ sarvasatvānaṁ ca hitasukhāya ||
shloka.translation: Inscribed upon the Mathura Lion Capital honoring all realms, the Śaka satraps dedicated stupas for the peace and welfare of all beings.
shloka.citation: Mathurā Lion Capital Kharoṣṭhī Inscription of Rājuvula (c. 10 CE)

shloka_epigraph.text: 𑀤𑁂𑀯𑀤𑁂𑀯𑀲 𑀯𑀸𑀲𑀼𑀤𑁂𑀯𑀲 𑀕𑀭𑀼𑀟𑀥𑁆𑀯𑀚𑁄 𑀅𑀬𑀁 𑀓𑀸𑀭𑀺𑀢𑁄 𑀇𑀬 𑀳𑁂𑀮𑀺𑀑𑀤𑁄𑀭𑁂𑀡 𑀪𑀸𑀕𑀯𑀢𑁂𑀦... 𑀢𑁆𑀭𑀻𑀦𑀺 𑀅𑀫𑀼𑀢𑀧𑀤𑀸𑀦𑀺 𑀲𑀼𑀅𑀦𑀼𑀞𑀺𑀢𑀸𑀦𑀺 𑀦𑀬𑀁𑀢𑀺 𑀲𑀕𑀁 — 𑀤𑀫𑁄 𑀘𑀸𑀕𑁄 𑀅𑀧𑁆𑀭𑀫𑀸𑀤𑁄 ॥
shloka_epigraph.translation: "This Garuda column of Vasudeva, the God of gods, was erected here by Heliodorus, a Bhagavata, son of Dion and inhabitant of Taxila, who came as Greek ambassador from King Antialcidas to King Bhagabhadra... Three are the immortal steps which lead to heaven when well observed: Self-restraint (Dama), Renunciation (Tyaga), and Vigilance (Apramada)."
shloka_epigraph.verified_from: Archaeological Survey of India, Annual Report 1908–1909, pp. 126–129

empires.historical_map_title: After the Mauryas — Shungas, Greeks and Sakas (c. 185 BCE–50 CE)

detailed_history.overview: The post-Mauryan epoch (c. 185 BCE – 50 CE) witnessed dynamic cross-cultural integration across northwestern and central India. While Pushyamitra Shunga founded the Shunga Dynasty at Pataliputra and Vidisha, revitalizing Vedic sacrificial rites (Ashvamedha) and patronizing Buddhist art at Bharhut, the Indo-Greek kings (Yavanas) under Menander I (Milinda) ruled Punjab, Gandhara, and the Kabul valley, fusing Hellenistic realism with Buddhist philosophy.

chronicle.era: c. 185 – 150 BCE: Pushyamitra Shunga & Vedic Restoration
chronicle.narrative: Pushyamitra Shunga, commander-in-chief (Senapati) of the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha, took the throne in 185 BCE. He celebrated two Ashvamedha horse sacrifices at Ayodhya, repelled incursions along the Sindhu river, and patronized the construction of the monumental stone railings and toranas at Bharhut Stupa.

chronicle.era: c. 165 – 130 BCE: Menander I (Milinda) & Greco-Buddhism
chronicle.narrative: From his capital at Sagala (Sialkot), the Greco-Bactrian king Menander I expanded his realm across Punjab and the Gangetic borders. His philosophical dialogues with the Buddhist monk Nagasena, recorded in the canonical Pali text Milindapañha, culminated in Menander embracing Buddhism and minting bilingual coins featuring the Greek legend and Kharosthi Prakrit 'Dharmikasa' (Follower of the Dharma).

chronicle.era: c. 115 – 50 BCE: Heliodorus Pillar & Cultural Syncretism
chronicle.narrative: In c. 113 BCE, the Greek king Antialcidas of Taxila dispatched ambassador Heliodorus to the court of King Bhagabhadra Shunga at Vidisha (Besnagar). Heliodorus dedicated a monolithic Garuda pillar to Vasudeva-Krishna, describing himself as a Bhagavata in early Brahmi script.

primary_sources.source_title: Heliodorus Garuda Pillar Inscription (Besnagar, Vidisha)
primary_sources.original_text: देवदेवस वासुदेवस गरुडध्वजे अयं कारिते इअ हेलियोदोरेण भागवतेन दियस पुत्रेण तखसिलाकेन योन-दूतेन आगतेन... त्रीणि अमृत-पदानि सु-अनुष्ठितानि नयंति स्वर्गं: दम त्याग अप्रमाद ॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Devadevasa Vāsudevasa garuḍadhvaje ayaṁ kārite ia Heliodoreṇa bhāgavatena Diyasa putreṇa Takhasilākena Yona-dūtena āgatena... Trīṇi amuta-padāni su-anuṣṭhitāni nayaṁti svagaṁ: dama tyāga apramāda ||
primary_sources.translation: This Garuda column of Vasudeva, the God of gods, was erected here by Heliodorus, a Bhagavata (devotee of Vishnu), son of Dion, an inhabitant of Taxila, who came as Greek ambassador from King Antialcidas to King Kasiputra Bhagabhadra... Three are the immortal steps which when well practiced lead to heaven: Self-restraint (Dama), Renunciation (Tyaga), and Vigilance (Apramada).
primary_sources.academic_citation: Archaeological Survey of India Annual Report 1908–1909, pp. 126–129; D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization, Vol. I, 1965, pp. 88–90.
primary_sources.significance: The oldest surviving monumental epigraphic proof of a Greek citizen adopting Vaishnava Hinduism and citing ethical tenets from the Mahabharata.

primary_sources.source_title: Ayodhyā Inscription of King Dhanadeva
primary_sources.original_text: कोसलाधिपेन द्विरश्वमेध-याजिनः सेनापतेः पुष्यमित्रस्य षष्ठेन... धनदेवेन धर्मराज्ञा पितुः फल्गुदेवस्य केतनं कारितम् ॥
primary_sources.transliteration: Kosalādhipena dvir-aśvamedha-yājinaḥ senāpateḥ Puṣyamitrasya ṣaṣṭhena... Dhanadevena dharmarājñā pituḥ Phalgudevasya ketanaṁ kāritam ||
primary_sources.translation: By the ruler of Kosala, Dhanadeva, the righteous king, sixth in descent from the Commander-in-Chief Pushyamitra who celebrated two Ashvamedha horse sacrifices, this memorial was caused to be made for his father Phalgudeva.
primary_sources.academic_citation: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. XX, p. 57; K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A Comprehensive History of India, Vol. II, Orient Longmans, 1957, pp. 95–98.
primary_sources.significance: Inscriptional confirmation of Pushyamitra Shunga's title Senapati and his celebration of two classical Vedic imperial sacrifices.

locations.name: Vidisha (Besnagar)
locations.role: Primary Shunga imperial capital and cultural center
locations.desc: Seat of Crown Prince Agnimitra; site of the Heliodorus Garuda pillar.

locations.name: Pataliputra
locations.role: Eastern Shunga imperial seat
locations.desc: Retained as imperial capital by Pushyamitra Shunga following the Mauryan overthrow.

locations.name: Sagala (Sialkot)
locations.role: Indo-Greek capital of King Menander I (Milinda)
locations.desc: Cosmopolitan Greco-Indian city celebrated for parks, moats, and Buddhist stupas in Milinda Panha.

locations.name: Pushkalavati (Charsadda)
locations.role: Western Indo-Greek mint and fortified administrative center
locations.desc: Center of Hellenistic minting and Gandharan stone craft.

locations.name: Taxila (Sirkap)
locations.role: Indo-Greek planned city built on Hippodamian grid
locations.desc: Sirkap urban phase featuring Greco-Bactrian temples, stupas, and bilingual coin mints.

locations.name: Mathura
locations.role: Easternmost Indo-Greek outpost and Shunga artistic center
locations.desc: Contested commercial hub where Indo-Greek drachms circulated alongside Shunga sculptures.

locations.name: Ayodhya (Saketa)
locations.role: Kosalan stronghold besieged by Greeks
locations.desc: Site of the Dhanadeva-Ayodhya inscription documenting Pushyamitra's two Ashvamedhas.

locations.name: Bharhut
locations.role: Famous Shunga-period Buddhist gateway and torana
locations.desc: Masterpiece of early Indian narrative stone relief sculpture inscribed 'Suganam Raje'.

locations.name: Sanchi
locations.role: Great Stupa enlarged with stone railings under the Shungas
locations.desc: Stone balustrade and toranas constructed during Shunga and Satavahana patronage.

locations.name: Alexandria in Arachosia (Kandahar)
locations.role: Indo-Greek western frontier stronghold
locations.desc: Greco-Bactrian military hub connecting Arachosia to the Indus basin.

locations.name: Demetrias in Sind
locations.role: Indo-Greek maritime harbor on the Indus mouth
locations.desc: Founded by Demetrius I to control Indian Ocean trade routes.

locations.name: Kaushambi
locations.role: Shunga administrative center on the Yamuna
locations.desc: Excavations revealed extensive Shunga brick fortifications, seals, and terracotta plaques.

empires.name: Satavahana Empire & Deccan Maritime Ascendancy
empires.era_type: Deccan Bridge & Indian Ocean Seaborne Trade
empires.religion: Brahmanical Hinduism (Vedic Yagnas) & Buddhist Stupa Patronage

capitals.name: Pratishthana (Paithan)
capitals.role: First imperial capital on the Godavari in Maharashtra
capitals.desc: Ancient textile and commercial center celebrated in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

capitals.name: Amaravati / Dharanikota
capitals.role: Eastern maritime capital on the Krishna River
capitals.desc: Magnificent Buddhist religious and artistic center; site of the Great Amaravati Stupa.

capitals.name: Junnar
capitals.role: Early western stronghold near Naneghat pass
capitals.desc: Surrounded by over 200 rock-cut caves and Buddhist viharas.

boundary_phases.phase: Early Andhra Consolidation under Satakarni I (c. 50 BCE)
boundary_phases.description: Early Satavahana dominion uniting upper Godavari (Pratishthana), Naneghat western Ghats pass, and coastal Andhra.
Deccan & Western Indian maritime empire stretching across Malwa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana, and coastal Andhra to the Bay of Bengal.

neighboring_kingdoms.name: Western Kshatrapas (Kshaharatas)
neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Indo-Scythian rulers of Gujarat, Malwa, and Saurashtra; issued refined silver coinage.

neighboring_kingdoms.name: Kushan Empire (North)
neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Kushan Empire (North): Contemporaneous frontier realm and trading partner.

neighboring_kingdoms.name: Sangam Kingdoms (South)
neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Sangam Kingdoms (South): Contemporaneous frontier realm and trading partner.

battles.name: Battle of Govardhana (Nashik)
battles.parties: Gautamiputra Satakarni vs. Nahapana (Western Kshatrapas)
battles.summary: Gautamiputra routed the Kshaharata satrap Nahapana, restriking thousands of his silver coins at the Jogalthambi hoard and liberating western Maharashtra.
battles.source: Nashik Cave Inscription No. 2 & Jogalthambi Coin Hoard

battles.name: Destruction of the Kshaharatas
battles.parties: Gautamiputra Satakarni vs. Kshaharata Remnants
battles.summary: Total extermination of the Kshaharata dynasty ('Kshaharata-vamsa-nirvaseshakara'), re-establishing Satavahana control over Konkan, Gujarat, and Malwa.

battles.name: Wars with Rudradaman I
battles.parties: Vashishtiputra Satakarni vs. Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman
battles.summary: Rudradaman defeated the Satavahana king twice in open field battle, but spared his life due to non-distant marital relationship, retaking Saurashtra and Aparanta.
battles.source: Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman, Lines 11–12

battles.name: Early Expansion into Malwa
battles.parties: Satakarni I vs. Shunga Regional Governors
battles.summary: Satakarni I crossed the Narmada and conquered western Malwa, minting coins at Ujjayini and celebrating two Ashvamedhas.

battles.name: Subjugation of the Kanvas
battles.parties: Satavahana Forces vs. King Susarman (Kanva)
battles.summary: Satavahana armies advanced into central India, slaying Susarman and annexing Vidisha and eastern territories.

battles.name: Naval Defense of the Western Seaboard
battles.parties: Yajna Sri Satakarni vs. Arab and Scythian Pirates
battles.summary: Maritime patrols secured the Indian Ocean trade lanes, commemorated on Yajna Sri Satakarni's famous ship-type lead and silver coins.
battles.source: Ship-Type Coin Corpus & Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

events.title: King Simuka Founds the Satavahana Dynasty at Pratishthana
events.desc: Establishes independent Andhra–Satavahana rule in the Godavari valley, creating an economic bridge between North India and Tamilakam.

shloka.text: माता भूमिः पुत्रो अहं पृथिव्याः ॥ पञ्च मानवीः प्रतिष्ठाने नित्यं धर्मं रक्षन्तु ॥
shloka.transliteration: mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṁ pṛthivyāḥ ||
shloka.translation: The Earth is my nurturing Mother, and I am a devoted son of this sacred soil—honoring Dakshinapatha from the banks of the Godavari.

events.title: Satakarni I & Queen Nayanika's Naneghat Pass Rock Inscription
events.desc: Commemorates two Ashvamedha and Rajasuya sacrifices, featuring the earliest stone portrait gallery and proto-Brahmi decimal numerals.

shloka.text: नमो धंमस नमो इंदस... वीरस सूरस अप्रतिहत-चक्कस दक्खिणापथ-पतिनो सातकणिस ॥
shloka.transliteration: Namo Dhaṁmasa namo Iṁdasa... vīrasa sūrasa apratihatacakasa Dakṣiṇāpathapatino Sātakaṇisa ||
shloka.translation: Salutation to Dharma and Indra... honoring the valiant, heroic, invincible sovereign Satakarni, Lord of Dakshinapatha.
shloka.citation: Nāneghāṭ Cave Inscription of Queen Nāganikā (Line 1–4)

events.title: Subjugation of Magadhan Kanvas & Malwa Trade Integration
events.desc: Satavahana armies push northward across the Narmada toward Vidisha, securing overland caravan access along the Dakshinapatha.

shloka.text: नर्मदातीरमासाद्य विन्ध्यपर्वतसन्निधौ । दक्षिणापथराजानः प्रापुः साम्राज्यगौरवम् ॥
shloka.transliteration: narmadātīramāsādya vindhyaparvatasannidhau | dakṣiṇāpatharājānaḥ prāpuḥ sāmrājyagauravam ||
shloka.translation: Securing the passes across the Vindhyas and Narmada, the sovereigns of Dakshinapatha unified the trunk trade arteries between Malwa and the Deccan.
shloka.citation: Matsya & Vāyu Purāṇa Satavahana Chronicle Tradition

events.title: King Hala Compiles the Maharashtri Prakrit Anthology Gāthā Sattasaī
events.desc: Seven hundred lyrical verses celebrating pastoral life, seasons, and rural affection across the Deccan plateau.

shloka.text: अमिअं पाअअकव्वं पढिउं सोउं च जे ण आणन्ति । कामस्स तत्ततत्तिं कुणन्ति ते कहं ण लज्जन्ति ॥
shloka.transliteration: Amiaṁ pāaakavvaṁ paḍhiuṁ souṁ ca je ṇa āṇanti | kāmassa tattatattiṁ kuṇanti te kahaṁ ṇa lajjanti ||
shloka.translation: Ambrosial is Prakrit poetry: those who know not how to read and savor these graceful verses miss the very essence of human tenderness and rustic beauty.

events.title: Monumental Excavation of the Great Chaitya at Karle & Kanheri Caves
events.desc: Merchants and guilds from Sopara and Kalyan carve the grandest Hinayana rock-cut Buddhist prayer halls in the Western Ghats.

shloka.text: वेजयन्तितो सेठिणा भूतपालेन सेलघरं परिनिठपितं जम्बुदीपम्हि उतमं ॥
shloka.transliteration: Vejayantito seṭhiṇā Bhūtapālena selagharaṁ pariniṭhapitaṁ Jaṁbudīpamhi utamaṁ ||
shloka.translation: By the merchant banker Bhutapala of Vaijayanti was this stone-hewn Chaitya monastery hall completed—the finest rock-cut mansion in all Jambudvipa.
shloka.citation: Kārle Great Chaitya Rock Inscription of Bhūtapāla

events.title: Periplus Seafaring & Konkan Guild Endowments across Kalyan & Junnar
events.desc: Western Ghats ports of Barygaza, Kalyan, and Chaul exchange Deccan cotton, agate beads, and pepper for Mediterranean glassware and silver.

shloka.text: सिधं । गोवर्धने श्रेणिनां धर्माक्षयनिवि दत्ता सार्थवाहानां हिताय सुखाय च ॥
shloka.transliteration: Sidhaṁ | Govardhane śreṇīnāṁ dharmākṣayanivi dattā sārthavāhānāṁ hitāya sukhāya ca ||
shloka.translation: Success! Perpetual endowment trusts (Akshayanivi) are deposited with weaver and potters' guilds at Govardhana to fund civic welfare permanently from interest.
shloka.citation: Nāsik Cave 10 Guild Endowment Inscription (Uṣavadāta Record)

events.title: Reign of Gautamiputra Satakarni & Battle of Govardhana (Nashik)
events.desc: Shatters the Kshaharata Saka power of Nahapana, counter-striking the 13,000-coin Jogalthambi silver hoard in victory.

shloka.text: सक-यवन-पल्हव-निसूदनस खखरात-वस-निरवसेस-करस सातवाहन-कुल-यस-पतिठापन-करस... तिसमुद-तोय-पीत-वाहनस ॥
shloka.transliteration: Saka-Yavana-Palhava-nisūdanasa Khakharāta-vasa-niravasesa-karasa Sātavāhana-kula-yasa-patiṭhāpana-karasa... tisamuda-toya-pīta-vāhanasa ||
shloka.translation: Destroyer of the Sakas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas; restorer of the Satavahana lineage; whose royal war-chargers drank from the waters of the three encircling oceans.
shloka.citation: Nāsik Cave 3 Inscription of Gautamī Balaśrī

events.title: Amaravati Great Stupa Enlarged under Vashishthiputra Pulumavi
events.desc: Shifts political weight toward Dharanikota on the Krishna river, adorning the Amaravati Mahachaitya in carved limestone reliefs.

shloka.text: धर्मो विश्वस्य जगतः प्रतिष्ठा लोके धर्मिष्ठं प्रजा उपसर्पन्ति । धर्मेण पापमपनुदन्ति धर्मे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितम् ॥
shloka.transliteration: dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā loke dharmiṣṭhaṁ prajā upasarpanti | dharmeṇa pāpam-apanudanti dharme sarvaṁ pratiṣṭhitam ||
shloka.translation: Dharma is the sustaining foundation of the entire cosmos; citizens gravitate toward the righteous guardian; all civilization stands anchored in Dharma.

events.title: Craft Town Prosperity at Paithan, Ter (Tagara) & Kondapur
events.desc: Terracotta artisans, bead-makers, and steel smelters along the upper Godavari and Manjira rivers power Deccan export guilds.

shloka.text: उद्योगिनं पुरुषसिंहमुपैति लक्ष्मीः दैवेन देयमिति कापुरुषा वदन्ति ॥
shloka.transliteration: udyoginaṁ puruṣasiṁham-upaiti lakṣmīḥ daivena deyam-iti kāpuruṣā vadanti ||
shloka.translation: Prosperity seeks out the energetic artisan and bold merchant guild; only the idle sit waiting passively for chance.

events.title: Diplomatic Marriage & Shaka–Satavahana Treaties at Girnar
events.desc: Western Kshatrapa King Rudradaman I notes twice sparing Vashishthiputra Satakarni because of close marital kinship.

shloka.text: दक्षिणापथपतेः सातकर्णेर्द्विरपि निर्व्याजमवजीत्यावजीत्य संबन्धविदूरताया अनुत्सादनात्प्राप्तयशसा ॥
shloka.transliteration: Dakṣiṇāpathapateḥ Sātakarṇer-dvir-api nirvyājam-avajītyā-vajītya saṁbandha-vidūratāyā anutsādanāt-prāptayaśasā ||
shloka.translation: Having twice fairly defeated Satakarni, Lord of Dakshinapatha, yet refraining from his utter destruction owing to close dynastic marriage ties.
shloka.citation: Junāgaḍh Rock Inscription of Rudradāman I (150 CE)

events.title: Yajna Sri Satakarni Mints Two-Masted Ship Coins for Maritime Trade
events.desc: Issues iconic silver and lead currency depicting rigged ocean-going vessels sailing from Sopara, Bharuch, and Ghantasala.

shloka.text: सिरि यञ सातकणिस ॥ यावद्द्वीपान्तरं याति नावा सागरगामिनी । तावद्राज्यं च वाणिज्यं समृद्धं भवति ध्रुवम् ॥
shloka.transliteration: Siri Yaña Sātakaṇisa (Ship Coin Legend) — nāvā sāgaragāminī vāṇijyaṁ samṛddhaṁ bhavati dhruvam ||
shloka.translation: Twin-masted lead and silver issues of Yajna Sri Satakarni celebrate Indian Ocean merchant fleets linking western Konkan ports with Coromandel and Suvarnabhumi.
shloka.citation: Yajña Śrī Sātakarṇi Bilingual Ship Coinage & Yuktikalpataru Tradition

events.title: Acharya Nagarjuna & Rise of the Sriparvata University at Nagarjunakonda
events.desc: Master philosopher Nagarjuna expounds Madhyamaka Shunyata along the Krishna Valley, laying foundations for Ikshvaku & Chalukya successors.

shloka.text: यः प्रतीत्यसमुत्पादं पश्यति इदं दुःखं तस्य समुदयं निरोधं मार्गं च स पश्यति ॥
shloka.transliteration: yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaṁ paśyati idaṁ duḥkhaṁ tasya samudayaṁ nirodhaṁ mārgaṁ ca sa paśyati ||
shloka.translation: Whoever sees interdependent origination perceives reality directly—freeing mind from extremes through balanced Middle Way wisdom.

shloka_epigraph.text: 𑀭𑀸𑀜𑁄 𑀕𑁄𑀢𑀫𑀻𑀧𑀼𑀢𑀲 𑀲𑀸𑀢𑀓𑀡𑀺𑀲... 𑀔𑀔𑀭𑀸𑀢𑀯𑀲𑀦𑀺𑀭𑁆𑀯𑀲𑁂𑀲𑀓𑀭𑀲 𑀲𑀸𑀢𑀯𑀸𑀳𑀦𑀓𑀼𑀮𑀬𑀲𑀧𑀢𑀺𑀞𑀸𑀧𑀦𑀓𑀭𑀲 𑀢𑁆𑀭𑀺𑀲𑀫𑀼𑀤𑁆𑀭𑀢𑁄𑀬𑀧𑀻𑀢𑀯𑀸𑀳𑀦𑀲 ॥
shloka_epigraph.translation: "Of King Gautamiputra Satakarni... who destroyed the pride and arrogance of the Kshatriyas, who completely eradicated the Kshaharata lineage, who restored the glory of the Satavahana dynasty, whose chargers drank the waters of the three oceans (Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, and Indian Ocean)."
shloka_epigraph.verified_from: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. VIII, pp. 60–65 (E. Senart, 1905)

sources.title: The Early History of the Deccan
sources.author: G. Yazdani

empires.historical_map_title: The Deccan Bridge — the Sātavāhana Age (c. 100 BCE–220 CE)

detailed_history.overview: The Sātavāhana Dynasty (Andhras, c. 100 BCE – 225 CE) ruled the Deccan plateau spanning Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh from twin capitals at Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati (Dhanyakataka). Guardians of the trans-peninsular trade routes linking the western ports (Kalyan, Sopara, Chaul) with the eastern Bay of Bengal, the Satavahanas were celebrated for their matronymic titles, cave temples at Karle, Kanheri, and Nasik, and the Great Stupa of Amaravati.

chronicle.era: c. 100 – 50 BCE: Simuka & Early Deccan Hegemony
chronicle.narrative: Simuka founded the dynasty in the Godavari basin following the decline of the Mauryas and Kanvas. Satakarni I performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and proclaimed himself Lord of the Southern Sea (Dakshinapathapati).

chronicle.era: c. 78 – 130 CE: Gautamiputra Satakarni & the Saka Wars
chronicle.narrative: The zenith of Satavahana power was achieved under Gautamiputra Satakarni (r. c. 106–130 CE), who annihilated the Kshaharata Saka dynasty of Nahapana, counter-striking his coins in the Jogalthambi hoard and restoring the religious and territorial sovereignty of the Deccan from Gujarat to Malwa and Krishna river.

chronicle.era: c. 130 – 225 CE: Vashishtiputra Pulumavi & Maritime Trade
chronicle.narrative: Successors Vashishtiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni minted coins featuring two-masted seafaring ships, demonstrating thriving oceanic commerce with the Roman Empire as documented in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

primary_sources.source_title: Nāsik Cave 3 Inscription of Gautami Balaśrī (Year 19 of Vāsiṣṭhīputra Puḷumāvi)
primary_sources.original_text: सक-यवन-पल्हव-निसूदनस खखरात-वस-निरवसेस-करस सातवाहन-कुल-यस-पतिठापन-करस... खतिय-दप-मान-मदनस एक-बम्हणस सिरि-गोतमिपुतस सातकणिस...
primary_sources.transliteration: Saka-Yavana-Palhava-nisūdanasa Khakharāta-vasa-niravasesa-karasa Sātavāhana-kula-yasa-patiṭhāpana-karasa... Khatiya-dapa-māna-madanasa eka-bamhaṇasa siri-Gotamiputasa Sātakaṇisa...
primary_sources.translation: Of the glorious Gautamiputra Satakarni, who crushed the pride of the Sakas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas; who eradicated the race of the Khaharata (Nahapana); who restored the glory of the Satavahana dynasty; who humbled the pride and arrogance of the Kshatriyas; the Unique Brahmana (Eka-Brahmana)... whose war steeds drank the waters of the three oceans (Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana).
primary_sources.academic_citation: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. VIII, pp. 60–65; Sudhakar Chattopadhyaya, The Sakas in India, Visva-Bharati, 1967, pp. 45–52.
primary_sources.significance: The primary royal eulogy detailing the complete geopolitical destruction of the Western Kshatrapas and the trans-oceanic domain of the Satavahana kingdom.

primary_sources.source_title: Junāgaḍh Rock Inscription of Rudradāman I (Girnar, Gujarat)
primary_sources.original_text: दक्षिणापथ-पतेः सातकर्णेर् द्विरपि निर्व्याजम् अवजीत्यावजीत्य संबन्ध-विदूरताया अनुत्सादनात् प्राप्त-यशसा...
primary_sources.transliteration: Dakṣiṇāpatha-pateḥ Sātakarṇer dvir-api nirvjyājam avajītyāvajītya saṁbandha-vidūratāyā anutsādanāt prāpta-yaśasā...
primary_sources.translation: Who, having twice in fair combat completely defeated Satakarni, the Lord of the Deccan (Dakshinapathapati), did not destroy him on account of the non-distant family relationship between them, and thereby gained great fame...
primary_sources.academic_citation: Epigraphia Indica, Vol. VIII, pp. 36–49; D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, Vol. I, pp. 175–186.
primary_sources.significance: The earliest lengthy Sanskrit prose inscription of undisputed date, recording royal diplomatic marriages and boundary wars between the Sakas and Satavahanas.

locations.name: Pratishthana (Paithan)
locations.role: First imperial capital on the Godavari in Maharashtra
locations.desc: Ancient textile and commercial center celebrated in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

locations.name: Amaravati / Dharanikota
locations.role: Eastern maritime capital on the Krishna River
locations.desc: Magnificent Buddhist religious and artistic center; site of the Great Amaravati Stupa.

locations.name: Junnar
locations.role: Early western stronghold near Naneghat pass
locations.desc: Surrounded by over 200 rock-cut caves and Buddhist viharas.

locations.name: Naneghat Pass
locations.role: Strategic mountain toll pass and royal inscription sanctuary
locations.desc: Queen Nayanika's Brahmi inscription recording Satakarni I's Vedic sacrifices and gifts.

locations.name: Karle (Karli)
locations.role: Greatest rock-cut Chaitya hall in ancient India
locations.desc: Grand wooden-ribbed rock architecture patronized by merchants and Satavahana kings.

locations.name: Sopara (Shurparaka)
locations.role: Major western port conducting maritime trade with Roman Egypt
locations.desc: Ancient port excavated with Roman amphorae and Ashokan rock edicts.

locations.name: Barygaza (Bharuch)
locations.role: Narmada estuary port described in the Periplus
locations.desc: Gateway for Roman gold, wine, and Italian glassware exchanged for Indian silk and pepper.

locations.name: Arikamedu (Podouke)
locations.role: Indo-Roman trading station on the Coromandel coast
locations.desc: Excavated with Arretine ware, Roman glass, rouletted pottery, and dyeing vats.

locations.name: Nagarjunakonda
locations.role: Major Buddhist university and monastery on the Krishna
locations.desc: Associated with philosopher Acharya Nagarjuna and patronized by Ikshvaku queens.

locations.name: Banavasi
locations.role: Southern Satavahana administrative stronghold in North Canara
locations.desc: Later became the capital of the Kadamba dynasty.

locations.name: Nashik (Pandavleni)
locations.role: Rock-cut monastic complex and royal eulogy site
locations.desc: Cave 3 contains Queen Gautami Balashri's famous prasasti celebrating Gautamiputra.

locations.name: Kanheri
locations.role: Foremost coastal Buddhist monastery near Mumbai
locations.desc: 109 rock-cut caves functioning as an educational and monastic center for 1,000 years.

locations.name: Ghantasala
locations.role: Eastern port mentioned by Ptolemy as Kontakossyla
locations.desc: Active maritime trade center carrying Buddhist pilgrims and spices to Sri Lanka.

empires.name: Kushan Empire & The Silk Road Synthesis
empires.era_type: Trans-Eurasian Crossroads of Gandhara Art & Commerce

capitals.name: Purushapura (Peshawar)
capitals.role: Winter imperial capital; site of Kanishka's Great Stupa
capitals.desc: Foremost Buddhist metropolis featuring Kanishka's 400-foot multi-tiered wooden stupa.

capitals.name: Mathura
capitals.role: Southern imperial capital and center of Indian art
capitals.desc: Cradle of the Mathura school of mottled red sandstone Buddhist, Jaina, and Brahmanical art.

capitals.name: Begram / Kapisa
capitals.role: Summer mountain capital in the Hindu Kush foothills
capitals.desc: Site of the spectacular Begram Treasure containing Chinese lacquer, Roman glassware, and Indian ivories.

capitals.name: Bactra / Balkh
capitals.role: Ancestral Northern capital and Silk Road crossroads
capitals.desc: Ancient mother of cities where Kushan emperors minted Greek-inscribed gold dinars.

boundary_phases.phase: Kujula & Vima Kadphises Bactrian–Gandharan Consolidation (c. 90 CE)
boundary_phases.description: Unified Yuezhi realm bridging Oxus valleys, Bactria, Gandhara, and Taxila with Roman-standard gold dinars.

boundary_phases.phase: Kanishka I's Silk Road & Gangetic Superpower (c. 140 CE)
boundary_phases.description: Eurasian crossroads uniting Transoxiana, Kashgar trade routes, Purushapura (Peshawar), Mathura, Kaushambi, and Pataliputra.

neighboring_kingdoms.desc: Han Dynasty / Western Regions: Contemporaneous frontier realm and trading partner.
